title: Don't Pay for Customers You Already Own
documentTitle: Email from Joan Braddi to Sundar Pichai et al. RE: Apple Response to Extension Term Length
excerptForBlog: We gave them a very generous offer without the ability to run numbers or ask how they plan to implement choice and us as the default. To Sundar's point, if they offer two types of browsers, one with Y and one with Google (even on the Mac side), we are just paying for loyal Google users which means that Apple added no value but insists on receiving 50% of the revenue. My opinion is to tell Steve our offer yesterday was very generous considering Apple has not discussed fully their plans nor how Google would be placed as default in these other applications to measure benefit to Google. I would hold firm. What Steve is asking is another 2.5 yrs for Mac and iPhone and 18 mos for Windows. I agree with Steve that fences need to be mended but it is Apple who needs to mend the fence. We have acted as partners in good faith and they have not. Good partners would have given us their plans and time to evaluate before setting a clock for our decision. I would let them try someone else for search if they don't like our last offer. Again, the Mac users are pretty loyal to Google. Again, these are negotiating tactics that Steve is famous for to get his terms. — Joan Braddi

lessonTitle: Don't Pay for Customers You Already Own
pullQuote: If your partner brings no real users to the deal, they aren't a partner — they're a toll booth.
leadershipTraits: reads tactics without taking them personally
situation: On June 7, 2007, Google executive Joan Braddi emailed Sundar Pichai, Sergey Brin, and Jonathan Rosenberg about an ongoing negotiation with Apple — likely over Google remaining the default search engine on Apple products. Apple's Steve Jobs was pushing for a longer extension and, implicitly, better revenue terms. The core tension: Google had already made what Braddi called 'a very generous offer' without Apple disclosing how it planned to implement search defaults.
insight: Braddi's email does one important thing: it separates Google's actual leverage from the emotional pressure of the relationship. She names the specific risk in Apple's ask — 'if they offer two types of browsers, one with Y and one with Google, we are just paying for loyal Google users' — which means Google would be buying distribution it doesn't need, because those users were already Google's. That is a classic switching-cost analysis run in reverse: if your customer's users aren't going anywhere anyway, you have pricing power, not the other way around. She also pattern-matches Steve Jobs's behavior directly, calling his pressure 'negotiating tactics that Steve is famous for.' That framing lets her team stay cool under what would otherwise feel like a high-stakes ultimatum. Her position — 'I would let them try someone else for search if they don't like our last offer' — is only credible because she believes Google's end-user loyalty is strong enough to survive a temporary loss of default placement. The document doesn't let us verify that assumption, but it is the load-bearing logic of her whole argument.
application: Before your next big negotiation, write down what your counterpart's users or customers would actually do if the deal fell through. If they'd largely stay with you anyway, your floor is higher than the pressure in the room suggests. Don't let relationship stakes or a ticking clock push you past that floor without new information that changes the underlying math.
